You will turn creative ideas into mechanical systems that can be manufactured, assembled, tested, transported, installed, and operated reliably in public spaces around the world. This is a hands-on mechanical design role for an engineer who enjoys unusual problems, rapid prototyping, close collaboration with fabrication and motion-control specialists, and seeing one-off systems operate at full scale. ‍The position can be filled at mid or senior level. We will assess level through the scale and complexity of the systems you have owned, your technical judgment, design-review and supplier responsibility, risk management, validation scope, and support for other engineers. ‍ In this role you will: Translate creative and project requirements into feasible mechanical concepts, kinematic layouts, dimensional studies, and first-order structural calculations. Take mechanisms and mechanical subsystems from concept through detailed design, prototyping, testing, and release. Design structures, motion-transmission systems, linkages, guides, drive mechanisms, tooling, jigs, and fixtures. Identify technical risks early, compare design alternatives, and define the prototypes or tests needed to validate critical assumptions. Make informed manufacturing and make-or-buy decisions based on performance, tolerance, quantity, cost, lead time, finish, and maintainability. Work directly with suppliers to source standard and custom components, resolve technical questions, and ensure manufacturability and quality. Produce clear manufacturing drawings, specifications, and accurate Bills of Materials that support traceable fabrication and assembly. Build and test prototypes using additive manufacturing and workshop processes, diagnose failures, and convert test results into design improvements. Support assembly, installation, and commissioning, define mechanical acceptance criteria, and verify that the finished system maintains the original design intent. Collaborate with fabrication, creative-technology, embedded, motion-control, and project teams while owning the mechanical design and its interfaces. At mid level, independently own defined mechanisms or mechanical subsystems, present design options and risks, coordinate suppliers, and support the assembly and commissioning of the systems you design. At senior level, own the mechanical architecture of complete installations or major systems. Lead feasibility, technical trade-offs, design reviews, supplier strategy, risk management, validation, and mechanical root-cause analysis, while supporting the development of other engineers. Must have: Demonstrated experience taking mechanisms, machines, or physical products through concept, detailed design, prototyping, testing, and release. Strong capability in parametric 3D mechanical CAD. Experience with Fusion 360 or Inventor is useful, but strong users of comparable platforms are welcome. Practical understanding of kinematics, mechanisms, motion transmission, structural sizing, materials, tolerances, and mechanical interfaces. Experience producing manufacturing-ready drawings, specifications, and accurate BOMs. Sound DFM/DFA and manufacturing-process selection judgment across several relevant methods, such as CNC machining, sheet metal, welding, additive manufacturing, molding, or specialist processes. Hands-on experience with prototyping, assembly, functional testing, and mechanical root-cause analysis. Ability to work pragmatically with suppliers, fabrication teams, assembly teams, and colleagues on site. English sufficient for technical collaboration and documentation, minimum B2. Willingness to work primarily from Leva’s Turin workshop and travel for installation and commissioning according to project requirements. Key skills: Strong practical engineering judgment, including the ability to work with incomplete or evolving requirements. Structured problem-solving and the ability to distinguish assumptions, risks, and verified findings. Ability to compare technical options and make pragmatic trade-offs between performance, cost, lead time, and reliability. Clear verbal and written communication with both technical and non-technical collaborators. Ownership of documentation, quality, and delivery—not only the CAD design. Adaptability without losing engineering rigor or traceability. Constructive collaboration across disciplines, with the confidence to challenge decisions when technical evidence requires it. Experience with surface-led geometry, kinetic installations, robotics, special machinery, exhibits, entertainment technology, or bespoke low-volume systems is useful but not required. Experience mechanically integrating motors, actuators, transmissions, guides, sensor mounts, and cable management is a plus. Controls programming is not required. Knowledge of GD&T, tolerance-stack analysis, FEA, fatigue, reliability, machine safety, or design for maintainability is welcome but optional. Experience with public-facing permanent installations, international suppliers, site work, or global commissioning is a plus. items.summary: The "old" version of Cowork runs model inference in the cloud, executing tool calls in an Anthropic-provided VM we shipped to your computer. We added the VM for capability, safety, and security reasons - mapping in just the data you explicitly added to your session. People loved what they were able to do with Claude but didn't love the disk, battery, and performance cost of running the VM locally. Also, people didn't love that closing your laptop means the work stops. The "new" version of Cowork runs model inference and the VM in the cloud. Each session gets its own sandbox, not sharing state with other sessions. When the VM needs something on the users' device (like a file), the desktop app is responsible for that file access tool call. items.title: Anthropic reported diary entry to police, woman faces felony charge
items.articleText: Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years. TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust . What just happened? Another incident has taken place that illustrates the need to be careful what you tell AI. A Florida woman is facing felony charges after she used Claude as a diary and allegedly wrote that she planned to "shoot up" the Sheriff's office. After a human reviewer examined the statements, they were reported to police. According to the arrest report , Carli Michelle Heller, of Bonita Springs, Florida, wrote on September 26 that she would attack the Sheriff's office. She later said that she uses Anthropic's chatbot like a "diary." Claude's safety systems flagged the entry and it was escalated to a human reviewer. After deciding it was a credible threat, the reviewer reported it to law enforcement. The company says it may share user information in limited emergencies if it believes disclosure is necessary to prevent death or serious physical injury. Deputies identified Heller and visited her home. She was detained without incident before an LCSO intelligence detective took over the investigation. Heller faces a charge of making a written threat of violence under Florida law. Florida Statute 836.10 makes it a second-degree felony to send, post, or transmit a written or electronic record threatening to kill or injure someone, carry out a mass shooting, or commit an act of terrorism. The communication must be made in a manner in which another person may view it. Anthropic isn't going to be taking any chances when it comes to anything it deems a potential threat. Last month, it was reported that OpenAI and Sam Altman are being sued by British Columbia over claims that the company could have prevented a mass shooting in the Canadian province. // Related Stories "The Big Short" investor says he's rooting for a crash just to stop OpenAI and Anthropic's IPOs Engineer says Claude Code has made his job "soul-sucking" as workers spend 12-hour days pressing enter The shooter, eighteen-year-old former pupil Jesse Van ⁠Rootselaar, had previously been flagged by OpenAI's safety team for her conversations about gun violence, but OpenAI never alerted police because the conversations did not meet the threshold for legal referral. In June, Florida also sued OpenAI and Altman, alleging that ChatGPT had contributed to real-world harms, including the 2025 Florida State University shooting. The latest incident is another reminder to think before you enter something into a chatbot that could get you into trouble. It's certainly not a private diary whose contents are for your eyes only. Reports last month revealed that human contractors reviewing Microsoft Copilot's image editor can see users' prompts, uploaded photos and AI-generated edits. Documents show that some of those assignments contain sexual, disturbing or potentially illegal material, though the reviewers are not there to flag the content – only to assess whether the output is accurate. 22 comments 11K likes and shares Share this article: See more TechSpot in Google Add us as a preferred source and our reporting shows up first when you search. items.articleText: Bright Factory is an intelligent manufacturing platform connecting design, automation, and data. | Source: Bright Machines Teradyne Inc. today announced a strategic investment in Bright Machines Inc., a builder of AI and data center infrastructure. The companies are also launching a strategic collaboration focused on integrating Teradyne robotics and test technologies with Bright Machines’ manufacturing platform. The move comes as Teradyne has been increasingly investing in AI across its ecosystem. In its most recent earnings statement , the North Reading, Mass.-based company marked its fifth consecutive quarter of growth. Teradyne credited AI as a main driver of its revenue growth. In addition, Universal Robots , a Teradyne subsidiary, recently released its seventh-generation cobot arm , which is designed to take advantage of AI advances. “Physical AI is changing what is possible on the factory floor, and Teradyne and Bright Machines are partnering to accelerate this evolution,” said Shantnu Sharma, chief development officer at Teradyne. “The combination of Bright Machines’ depth in software-defined manufacturing and Teradyne’s decades of experience in robotics and test gives companies building AI infrastructure a faster path from design into production, with data behind every unit they build.” Teradyne and Bright Machines jointly automate production The partners said they plan to integrate Teradyne’s technologies into Bright Machines’ production environments. This will include precision robotic assembly , robotic loading and unloading of test equipment, and autonomous movement of materials. The companies hope to deploy the technology at Bright Machines’ and customer sites. At these sites, the Bright Machines manufacturing platform , Universal Robots’ force- and power-limited robots , and Teradyne’s board test systems would operate together on a production floor. Each produces a distinct stream of information: assembly and inspection data, robot and material-movement data, and electrical test results. “By connecting these data streams with Bright Machines’ product genealogy and manufacturing intelligence capabilities, customers can maintain an end-to-end production data thread linking design decisions, assembly execution, and electrical performance,” asserted Teradyne. “What limits automation today is not what a robot can physically do but how much engineering it takes to tell it what to do,” said James Davidson, chief AI officer at Teradyne. “When a robot can pick up a new task in hours instead of being re-engineered over weeks, high-mix, short lifecycle production becomes the default. Once build data and test data sit in the same loop, the line can correct itself quickly.” Teradyne noted that AI infrastructure is demanding. Product complexity is high, design cycles are short, quality requirements are stringent, and schedules leave little room for rework. Manufacturers serving this market increasingly value an integrated approach spanning manufacturing design, intelligent robotics, autonomous material handling, quality assurance, and end-to-end production intelligence, delivered as one coordinated system. “The next generation of AI infrastructure calls for a manufacturing approach that is more automated, software-defined, data-driven, and responsive to change,” stated Sviat Dulianinov, CEO of Bright Machines. “Teradyne’s expertise, and the investment that comes with it, helps us validate that approach. Their robotics and test technologies are complementary to our platform, and together we can help customers simplify integration, accelerate deployment, and maintain a complete production data thread.” Partners share AI infrastructure experience AI infrastructure is driving one of the largest electronics manufacturing buildouts in recent history, noted Teradyne. As hyperscalers, AI laboratories, silicon providers, and OEMs invest in next-generation compute, manufacturing has become a determinant of deployment speed, quality, and economic value, it added. Manufacturers place a premium on lines that can be reconfigured in software as product designs refresh. Teradyne claimed that it is working with manufacturers across that ecosystem, including electronics manufacturing services (EMS) and original design manufacturer (ODM) providers, OEMs, and hyperscalers. It said it supplies robotics and test technologies to make high-mix, high-value electronics production possible. Burlingame, Calif.-based Bright Machines brings a software-defined manufacturing platform spanning design, robotics, automation, inspection, material movement, production intelligence, and operations. items.title: FCC robot restrictions could accelerate shift to local AI
items.summary: Companies deploying physical AI today need to decide which AI workloads belong on the robot, what can remain in the cloud, and whether the underlying technology stack can meet rising expectations for security, safety, and supply-chain transparency. The post FCC robot restrictions could accelerate shift to local AI appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: A Unitree humanoid robot at the China Humanoid Robot Conference in Seoul in March. Robots are back in the national spotlight, and this time, the conversation is about more than what they can do. It’s about who controls them and what data they collect. The restrictions on foreign-produced robots by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) underscore the growing scrutiny of these machines as connected infrastructure. As robots take on more work in factories, warehouses, and other high-stakes environments, questions about how they use data and make decisions are becoming harder to ignore. That scrutiny is likely to accelerate the move toward on-premises AI architectures and smaller, specialized models that can run closer to where robots operate. The more control companies want over who can access a robot and its data, the more incentive they have to keep sensitive processing close to the machine. Companies deploying physical AI today need to decide which AI workloads belong on the robot, what can remain in the cloud, and whether the underlying technology stack can meet rising expectations for security, safety, and supply-chain transparency. Robot security is becoming an architecture question In July, the FCC added foreign-produced advanced robotic devices to a list of technologies it deems to pose unacceptable national security or safety risks. That designation prevents new devices from receiving the FCC authorization generally required to be imported, marketed, or sold in the U.S. The restrictions apply broadly to advanced mobile robots, including humanoids and quadrupeds, that can collect detailed information about the environments around them. Officials have warned that foreign-made robots could give foreign actors a way to conduct surveillance, collect sensitive data, or remotely interfere with machines operating inside American facilities. But hardware origin is only one part of the security equation. If a robot is continuously collecting information about a facility and sending it to an external cloud service for processing, companies also have to consider where that data goes and who can access it. Editor’s Note: The Robot Report is hosting a free webinar on October 27 called “The FCC Robotics Ruling: What Automation Buyers Need to Know .” Join leaders from Vecna Robotics , Locus Robotics and the Association for Advancing Automation (A3) for a discussion about what the FCC action means for the robotics industry and the organizations investing in automation. Moving intelligence closer to the robot Keeping more inference on the robot or inside a facility was already attractive because it improves latency and reliability. The recent regulatory change could make local processing a higher priority for a broader range of AI workloads, especially those involving internal operational data. For core control functions such as motion control and safety monitoring, local processing is non-negotiable. The bigger change is likely to happen higher in the stack, where robots interpret instructions, analyze their surroundings, respond to anomalies, and make task-level decisions. Those workloads can be computationally intensive, and the cloud offers more processing power than most edge hardware. But relying on external cloud resources can introduce network dependence and require operational data to leave the facility. Companies will likely need to run more of that intelligence locally within tighter compute limits. Explore our database of 200+ humanoid robotics companies from around the world. Why SLMs could gain ground The more organizations move higher-level intelligence on-device, the less practical it becomes to rely on cloud-dependent large language models (LLMs) for every task. That strengthens the case for small language models (SLMs) designed for industrial environments. A robot operating in a defined environment doesn’t always need a model built to handle almost any question. It needs one that understands the context of the facility and can perform the tasks required there reliably. That doesn’t mean the robot has to be locked into a single job. With the right context and access to local data, an SLM can support a wider range of applications within the same facility. For example, a robotic arm working on one production line could be moved elsewhere in the factory and adapted to perform a similar task in a different production environment. SLMs can be fine-tuned on a factory’s own data and run directly on edge hardware with lower compute requirements than larger general-purpose models. For many industrial use cases, the combination of specialization and flexibility across changing local deployments can make them a stronger fit for the job. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! More local control means more integration work These changes raise the bar for system design at U.S. companies building or integrating robots. You must ensure that controllers, sensors, safety systems, and AI hardware can work together reliably and that the full system can be secured and maintained over time. When you buy a finished robot, many integration and certification decisions have already been made. Building one from components puts more of the engineering burden on your organization: How will components be integrated? How will safety be validated? How will firmware be maintained, and where will critical parts come from? The right suppliers can help answer those questions with tested components, traceable sourcing, and deployment support. U.S. businesses need suppliers that can show how their components have been tested together, document where critical parts come from, and provide the safety and governance support needed after deployment. When those pieces have already been validated to work together, builders can spend less time solving component-level integration problems and more time focusing on the complete system. Building for control from the start The most immediate effect of the FCC action is on sourcing. Its longer-term impact may be even bigger: architecture. As robots move deeper into sensitive and mission-critical environments, companies will have to evaluate them on more than capability or performance. They need to know whether critical processing can stay local, where robot data is going, and how much confidence they can place in the underlying components. Businesses that build those controls in from the start will be better positioned to deploy physical AI without creating problems they have to unwind later. entries.title: Anthropic Claude Cowork, 로컬 VM 방식에서 클라우드 샌드박스 아키텍처로 개편
entries.reason: 로컬 가상머신 구동으로 인한 배터리·디스크 소모와 세션 중단 문제를 클라우드 격리 샌드박스와 데스크톱 로컬 파일 브리지로 해결한 구조 변경을 설명합니다.

facts.statement: 새 버전의 Cowork는 모델 추론과 VM 실행을 클라우드 샌드박스에서 독립적으로 처리하며, 로컬 파일 접근이 필요할 때만 데스크톱 앱이 도구 호출을 수행하도록 변경되었습니다.
facts.quote: The "new" version of Cowork runs model inference and the VM in the cloud. Each session gets its own sandbox, not sharing state with other sessions. When the VM needs something on the users' device (like a file), the desktop app is responsible for that file access tool call.

entries.title: Qwen3.8-27B 로컬 모델의 단어 표기 덧셈 벤치마크 실험 결과
entries.reason: 양자화된 로컬 오픈 가중치 언어 모델이 추론(Reasoning) 활성화 여부에 따라 큰 자릿수 텍스트 덧셈 연산에서 보이는 정확도 차이를 확인할 수 있습니다.

facts.statement: Qwen3.8-27B 양자화 모델은 추론 비활성화 시 23.57%의 수치 정확도를 보였으나, 추론 활성화 시 169회 시도 중 167회 정답을 기록했습니다.
facts.quote: Without reasoning, it achieved 23.57% numeric accuracy, with performance dropping from 97.04% for one- to three-digit operands to 6.44% for ten- to thirteen-digit operands

This week’s meeting was held on 2026-10-05T18:00:00Z and the following is a summary: PMC Business PMC Membership & Mentee Committer Voting : Voting is currently open for adding Cherry as a mentee committer, and an asynchronous email vote is being opened for Luca Della Vedova’s nomination to the PMC. Asynchronous Meeting Engagement : The PMC agreed to encourage members and contributors in conflicting time zones to participate asynchronously by adding agenda items and updates directly to the meeting agenda document or discussing topics on Zulip. Process for Inactive Members : The committee discussed procedures for handling inactive PMC members and committers to prevent quorum issues. The PMC agreed to research official processes while prioritizing informal outreach to overburdened members first to ask if they wish to step down. New agenda items Phase 2 of Gazebo Maintainer Audit & Rebalancing : Phase 2 of the maintainer audit is currently underway with a due date of 2026-10-16T00:00:00Z . Contributors interested in maintaining a project are encouraged to sign up on the Maintainer Audit & Rebalancing Workspace (2026) (not public) . Multiple individuals can sign up for the same project; final assignments will be rebalanced across the team at the end of Phase 2. Introduction to rosdistro-extension and its Impact on Gazebo : A presentation was given on the rosdistro-extension project , which extends the ROS Distro metadata index and Python library. This project explores allowing ROS distributions to consume Gazebo packages directly through source imports (where ROS rebuilds packages from source, e.g., ROS Rolling extending Gazebo Jetty) and binary imports. While this could potentially replace Gazebo vendor packages in ROS and simplify release maintenance, CMake shims and upstream CI testing will still need to be addressed. Handling Unreleased Breaking Changes in gz-rendering and gz-sensors : Following changes in gazebosim/gz-rendering#1331 , a newly added image constructor was backported and later deprecated in stable branches. Because this function was never part of an official release, the PMC aligned on removing it directly from Jetty (and verifying other stable branches) rather than keeping an unreleased deprecated function, addressing warnings like gazebosim/gz-sensors#675 . Automating “Build Bottle” in Release Tooling : The team discussed gazebo-tooling/release-tools#1560 regarding automating the build bottle step when running release.py for Homebrew simulation pull requests. Consensus was reached to automate this step while implementing guardrails (such as detecting existing tags or PRs) to prevent duplicate script runs and duplicate PRs. Gazebo Mosaic Next Steps : With the community naming process concluding and “Mosaic” selected as the name for the Gazebo M release, next steps for finalizing the naming rollout and repository setup will be coordinated. Updates Buildfarm & CI The Greenness report continues to show strong test coverage (>90–95%). Written Updates (Not Discussed Live) The following items were submitted as written updates in the agenda but were not discussed live during the meeting due to time constraints: Package Updates gz-sim : Added detection for WindowServer and Metal support on macOS in FindDRI (gazebosim/gz-sim#4036 , currently in review), eliminating the need for XQuartz on macOS. Preparing for a second round of prereleases for Rotary. gz-rendering : Stabilizing Image changes in main and released branches. gz-transport : Preparing a PR for Jetty with Zenoh backports and two manual fixes for ABI compatibility. sdformat : A PR is awaiting review to support URDF 1.1 capsules in SDFormat (gazebosim/sdformat#1722 ). Note: the urdfdom version in bazel-central-registry is currently outdated. gz-cmake : Added REQUIRE support (gazebosim/gz-cmake#595 ). Suppressed warnings when optional components are not found, fixing CMake issues in gz-sensors when the gz-rendering ogre1 component is absent (gazebosim/gz-cmake#587 ). Release Tooling & Infrastructure release-tools : Started work on supporting parameterless execution of release.py (gazebo-tooling/release-tools#1564 ). Improving the auto-changelog generator tool to handle backports with squash/rebase (gazebo-tooling/release-tools#1447 ). Drafting Pixi support for macOS CI. selectedItems.summary: The companies plan to integrate Teradyne robotics and test technologies with the Bright Machines manufacturing platform. The post Teradyne invests in Bright Machines to bring robotics to AI infrastructure manufacturing appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: Bright Factory is an intelligent manufacturing platform connecting design, automation, and data. | Source: Bright Machines Teradyne Inc. today announced a strategic investment in Bright Machines Inc., a builder of AI and data center infrastructure. The companies are also launching a strategic collaboration focused on integrating Teradyne robotics and test technologies with Bright Machines’ manufacturing platform. The move comes as Teradyne has been increasingly investing in AI across its ecosystem. In its most recent earnings statement , the North Reading, Mass.-based company marked its fifth consecutive quarter of growth. Teradyne credited AI as a main driver of its revenue growth. In addition, Universal Robots , a Teradyne subsidiary, recently released its seventh-generation cobot arm , which is designed to take advantage of AI advances. “Physical AI is changing what is possible on the factory floor, and Teradyne and Bright Machines are partnering to accelerate this evolution,” said Shantnu Sharma, chief development officer at Teradyne. “The combination of Bright Machines’ depth in software-defined manufacturing and Teradyne’s decades of experience in robotics and test gives companies building AI infrastructure a faster path from design into production, with data behind every unit they build.” Teradyne and Bright Machines jointly automate production The partners said they plan to integrate Teradyne’s technologies into Bright Machines’ production environments. This will include precision robotic assembly , robotic loading and unloading of test equipment, and autonomous movement of materials. The companies hope to deploy the technology at Bright Machines’ and customer sites. At these sites, the Bright Machines manufacturing platform , Universal Robots’ force- and power-limited robots , and Teradyne’s board test systems would operate together on a production floor. Each produces a distinct stream of information: assembly and inspection data, robot and material-movement data, and electrical test results. “By connecting these data streams with Bright Machines’ product genealogy and manufacturing intelligence capabilities, customers can maintain an end-to-end production data thread linking design decisions, assembly execution, and electrical performance,” asserted Teradyne. “What limits automation today is not what a robot can physically do but how much engineering it takes to tell it what to do,” said James Davidson, chief AI officer at Teradyne. “When a robot can pick up a new task in hours instead of being re-engineered over weeks, high-mix, short lifecycle production becomes the default. Once build data and test data sit in the same loop, the line can correct itself quickly.” Teradyne noted that AI infrastructure is demanding. Product complexity is high, design cycles are short, quality requirements are stringent, and schedules leave little room for rework. Manufacturers serving this market increasingly value an integrated approach spanning manufacturing design, intelligent robotics, autonomous material handling, quality assurance, and end-to-end production intelligence, delivered as one coordinated system. “The next generation of AI infrastructure calls for a manufacturing approach that is more automated, software-defined, data-driven, and responsive to change,” stated Sviat Dulianinov, CEO of Bright Machines. “Teradyne’s expertise, and the investment that comes with it, helps us validate that approach. Their robotics and test technologies are complementary to our platform, and together we can help customers simplify integration, accelerate deployment, and maintain a complete production data thread.” Partners share AI infrastructure experience AI infrastructure is driving one of the largest electronics manufacturing buildouts in recent history, noted Teradyne. As hyperscalers, AI laboratories, silicon providers, and OEMs invest in next-generation compute, manufacturing has become a determinant of deployment speed, quality, and economic value, it added. Manufacturers place a premium on lines that can be reconfigured in software as product designs refresh. Teradyne claimed that it is working with manufacturers across that ecosystem, including electronics manufacturing services (EMS) and original design manufacturer (ODM) providers, OEMs, and hyperscalers. It said it supplies robotics and test technologies to make high-mix, high-value electronics production possible. Burlingame, Calif.-based Bright Machines brings a software-defined manufacturing platform spanning design, robotics, automation, inspection, material movement, production intelligence, and operations. The company has deployed more than 130 microfactories across over 10 countries and active AI infrastructure production in the U.S. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! selectedItems.title: FCC robot restrictions could accelerate shift to local AI
selectedItems.summary: Companies deploying physical AI today need to decide which AI workloads belong on the robot, what can remain in the cloud, and whether the underlying technology stack can meet rising expectations for security, safety, and supply-chain transparency. The post FCC robot restrictions could accelerate shift to local AI appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: A Unitree humanoid robot at the China Humanoid Robot Conference in Seoul in March. Robots are back in the national spotlight, and this time, the conversation is about more than what they can do. It’s about who controls them and what data they collect. The restrictions on foreign-produced robots by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) underscore the growing scrutiny of these machines as connected infrastructure. As robots take on more work in factories, warehouses, and other high-stakes environments, questions about how they use data and make decisions are becoming harder to ignore. That scrutiny is likely to accelerate the move toward on-premises AI architectures and smaller, specialized models that can run closer to where robots operate. The more control companies want over who can access a robot and its data, the more incentive they have to keep sensitive processing close to the machine. Companies deploying physical AI today need to decide which AI workloads belong on the robot, what can remain in the cloud, and whether the underlying technology stack can meet rising expectations for security, safety, and supply-chain transparency. Robot security is becoming an architecture question In July, the FCC added foreign-produced advanced robotic devices to a list of technologies it deems to pose unacceptable national security or safety risks. That designation prevents new devices from receiving the FCC authorization generally required to be imported, marketed, or sold in the U.S. The restrictions apply broadly to advanced mobile robots, including humanoids and quadrupeds, that can collect detailed information about the environments around them. Officials have warned that foreign-made robots could give foreign actors a way to conduct surveillance, collect sensitive data, or remotely interfere with machines operating inside American facilities. But hardware origin is only one part of the security equation. If a robot is continuously collecting information about a facility and sending it to an external cloud service for processing, companies also have to consider where that data goes and who can access it. Editor’s Note: The Robot Report is hosting a free webinar on October 27 called “The FCC Robotics Ruling: What Automation Buyers Need to Know .” Join leaders from Vecna Robotics , Locus Robotics and the Association for Advancing Automation (A3) for a discussion about what the FCC action means for the robotics industry and the organizations investing in automation. Moving intelligence closer to the robot Keeping more inference on the robot or inside a facility was already attractive because it improves latency and reliability. The recent regulatory change could make local processing a higher priority for a broader range of AI workloads, especially those involving internal operational data. For core control functions such as motion control and safety monitoring, local processing is non-negotiable. The bigger change is likely to happen higher in the stack, where robots interpret instructions, analyze their surroundings, respond to anomalies, and make task-level decisions. Those workloads can be computationally intensive, and the cloud offers more processing power than most edge hardware. But relying on external cloud resources can introduce network dependence and require operational data to leave the facility. Companies will likely need to run more of that intelligence locally within tighter compute limits. Explore our database of 200+ humanoid robotics companies from around the world. Why SLMs could gain ground The more organizations move higher-level intelligence on-device, the less practical it becomes to rely on cloud-dependent large language models (LLMs) for every task. That strengthens the case for small language models (SLMs) designed for industrial environments. A robot operating in a defined environment doesn’t always need a model built to handle almost any question. It needs one that understands the context of the facility and can perform the tasks required there reliably. That doesn’t mean the robot has to be locked into a single job. With the right context and access to local data, an SLM can support a wider range of applications within the same facility. For example, a robotic arm working on one production line could be moved elsewhere in the factory and adapted to perform a similar task in a different production environment. SLMs can be fine-tuned on a factory’s own data and run directly on edge hardware with lower compute requirements than larger general-purpose models. For many industrial use cases, the combination of specialization and flexibility across changing local deployments can make them a stronger fit for the job. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! More local control means more integration work These changes raise the bar for system design at U.S. companies building or integrating robots. You must ensure that controllers, sensors, safety systems, and AI hardware can work together reliably and that the full system can be secured and maintained over time. When you buy a finished robot, many integration and certification decisions have already been made. Building one from components puts more of the engineering burden on your organization: How will components be integrated? How will safety be validated? How will firmware be maintained, and where will critical parts come from? The right suppliers can help answer those questions with tested components, traceable sourcing, and deployment support. U.S. businesses need suppliers that can show how their components have been tested together, document where critical parts come from, and provide the safety and governance support needed after deployment. When those pieces have already been validated to work together, builders can spend less time solving component-level integration problems and more time focusing on the complete system. Building for control from the start The most immediate effect of the FCC action is on sourcing. Its longer-term impact may be even bigger: architecture. As robots move deeper into sensitive and mission-critical environments, companies will have to evaluate them on more than capability or performance. They need to know whether critical processing can stay local, where robot data is going, and how much confidence they can place in the underlying components. Businesses that build those controls in from the start will be better positioned to deploy physical AI without creating problems they have to unwind later. About the Author Jenny Shern, general manager at NexCOBOT , is responsible for managing the company’s sales and business strategy, robotic and motion control product development and project deployment. Shern specializes in building strategic partnerships and business development in IoT automation, robotics and retail sectors. She previously worked at NEXCOM from 2005 to 2018, where she led sales teams in building global channel network and multi-national automation key account customers. In 2018, NexCOBOT spun off from NEXCOM IoT Automation Solutions Business Group, focusing on providing open robotic and machine control systems for industrial and collaborative robot applications.
